I am preparing a research survey on reasoning capabilities in large language models and I need your help gathering information and producing a report. Please search for recent academic papers that deal with reasoning in large language models, covering topics such as chain-of-thought prompting, tree-based deliberation, self-consistency methods, process supervision for mathematical reasoning, and reinforcement learning approaches to scaling reasoning. I expect there to be around five relevant papers on these topics in the database.

For each paper you find, please retrieve the full details including title, authors, abstract, and any available content. I also need you to look up citation counts and publication venue information for these papers through a scholarly search. Additionally, please examine the source manuscripts of the papers to read their methodology sections in detail, as this will be important for the comparison section of the report.

Once you have gathered all the necessary information, please create a Word document called LLM_Reasoning_Survey.docx in my workspace. The document should have a title at the top reading "Survey: Reasoning Capabilities in Large Language Models" followed by four main sections. The first section should be an Introduction that provides an overview of the field of reasoning in large language models and explains why this area of research is significant. The second section should be a Literature Review that summarizes each of the papers you found, clearly stating for each paper its title, authors, key contribution, citation count, and publication venue. The third section should be a Methodology Comparison that analyzes and contrasts the different approaches taken across the papers you reviewed, discussing how each method addresses the challenge of improving reasoning in language models. The fourth and final section should be a Conclusion that synthesizes the main findings, identifies common themes, and discusses potential future directions for research in this area.

After creating the Word document, please also export or convert it to a PDF file named LLM_Reasoning_Survey.pdf in the same workspace directory. Both files should be present when you are finished.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently, follow this exact orchestration plan. A wave must finish and return all stated handoffs before the next wave begins. Within a wave, dispatch exactly one sub-agent for each numbered sub-task and run those sub-agents concurrently.

Before Wave 1, the main agent must freeze five non-overlapping topic slots from the task—chain-of-thought, tree-based deliberation, self-consistency, process supervision, and reinforcement-learning approaches to scaling reasoning—and the exact Word/PDF section and filename contract. It must derive titles, IDs, venues, citations, and benchmark numbers only from task-visible runtime sources. It must also resolve the task-visible workspace directory from the runtime allowed-directory listing (or the literal accessible-workspace directory already supplied by the harness), freeze `<workspace_root>`, and reject bare `/workspace` and dumps/run-specific paths.

1. Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 5 sub-agents in parallel, one for each numbered sub-task:

   1. explore 0 (academic-literature-researcher 0): Use one explore sub-agent to research chain-of-thought prompting.
   2. explore 1 (academic-literature-researcher 1): Use one explore sub-agent to research tree-based deliberation.
   3. explore 2 (academic-literature-researcher 2): Use one explore sub-agent to research self-consistency.
   4. explore 3 (academic-literature-researcher 3): Use one explore sub-agent to research process supervision for mathematical reasoning.
   5. explore 4 (academic-literature-researcher 4): Use one explore sub-agent to research reinforcement-learning approaches to scaling reasoning.

Each Wave 1 sub-agent must search the arXiv and Scholarly collections read-only for its assigned topic, validate relevance by title/abstract, cross-reference venue and numeric citation count by normalized title, and inspect the available arxiv-latex methodology and experiment sections. Return one compact record for the strongest non-overlapping paper with stable ID, title, full authors, abstract, venue, citation count, method, source-backed results, section coverage, provenance, query/source controls, and missing/conflict status; if no genuine paper exists, record that rather than inventing one. Explore is read-only, so do not write files or create the survey files.

After Wave 1, the main agent must deduplicate IDs/titles, verify one genuinely relevant paper per topic where the runtime sources support it, resolve venue/citation conflicts by provenance, and freeze one literal canonical survey packet using only task-visible runtime evidence. The DOCX and PDF must consume this same packet; no export branch may re-research or recompute claims.

2. Wave 2 — dispatch exactly 1 sub-agent for the following numbered sub-task:

   1. coder 0 (office-report-builder 0): Use one coder sub-agent to own both `<workspace_root>/LLM_Reasoning_Survey.docx` and its dependent `<workspace_root>/LLM_Reasoning_Survey.pdf` exclusively. Create the Word document exactly once with the exact title and four main sections, include every frozen paper's authors, contribution, citation count, venue, and source-backed methodology comparison, and then read it back. Only after DOCX validation, call the authorized Word-to-PDF conversion once for the exact PDF filename. If that converter fails because LibreOffice/soffice/docx2pdf is unavailable, use `python_execute` once with the installed `python-docx` and `reportlab` packages to read the verified DOCX as the sole source and render the same headings, paragraphs, and tables into the exact PDF path; this is a true PDF generation fallback, not a renamed file or an independently rewritten survey. Then call the PDF information and page-reading tools, require a readable PDF larger than 5 KB with the title and all four section headings, and return both paths, heading/paper coverage, word/page controls, conversion route, and validation. Do not let any other agent write either file.

After Wave 2, the main agent must verify that both files exist, are readable, contain the same frozen paper set and four-section narrative, and that the PDF was produced from the verified DOCX by the primary converter or the declared pure-Python fallback. If neither route creates a valid PDF, retain the DOCX and report the exact blocker without claiming completion. Complete only after both deliverables pass the integrity checks.

CONTENTS (exact order):

=== TITLE (style "Title") ===
Survey: Reasoning Capabilities in Large Language Models

=== HEADING 1 ===
Introduction

=== Paragraph I1 ===
Large language models (LLMs) have transformed natural language processing, yet multi-step reasoning—the ability to decompose a problem into intermediate steps that lead to a correct conclusion—remains one of the central frontiers of the field. Rather than mapping inputs directly to answers, a reasoning-capable model must carry out arithmetic, symbolic, or commonsense inference one step at a time. Understanding, eliciting, and scaling this ability is significant because it determines whether LLMs can be trusted in high-stakes domains such as mathematics, scientific discovery, software engineering, and autonomous decision-making, and because reasoning performance has become one of the clearest measurable indicators of progress toward more general machine intelligence.

=== Paragraph I2 ===
What makes this research area distinctive is that progress has arrived through qualitatively different mechanisms. A first wave of work showed that reasoning can be elicited purely through prompt engineering, by asking models to write out intermediate steps, known as chains of thought. A second wave amplified reasoning at inference time using richer sampling and search procedures that let the model explore multiple lines of reasoning instead of committing to the first one it generates. A third wave improved the models themselves by introducing better supervision signals and reinforcement learning, transferring reasoning capability from clever inference-time procedures into the model's weights. Taken together, these threads trace an arc from eliciting reasoning, to amplifying it, to verifying it, and finally to learning it.

=== Paragraph I3 ===
This survey reviews five representative papers that span those mechanisms: chain-of-thought prompting, tree-of-thoughts search, self-consistency decoding, process supervision for mathematical reasoning, and reinforcement learning for scaling reasoning. For each paper we summarize the key contribution, citation metrics, and publication venue, and we analyze the methodologies in detail, comparing how each approach addresses the shared challenge of improving reasoning in language models.

=== HEADING 1 ===
Literature Review

=== Paragraph LR0 ===
Five papers retrieved from the scholarly database are reviewed below. Citation counts and venues were obtained through a scholarly search and reflect the values returned at the time of the search.

=== HEADING 2 ===
Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models

=== Paragraph LR1a ===
This paper, authored by Jason Wei and Xuezhi Wang, was published at NeurIPS and has accumulated 850 citations according to the scholarly search. It is widely regarded as the foundational work that established prompting as a mechanism for eliciting reasoning in large language models.

=== Paragraph LR1b ===
The key contribution is chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting: each few-shot exemplar is augmented from a simple input–output pair into an input–chain of thought–answer triple, where the chain of thought is a series of intermediate natural-language reasoning steps. By imitating the decomposition patterns in the exemplars, the model learns to reason step by step before answering. Crucially, the method requires no training or fine-tuning—it is purely a prompt-design intervention—and its benefits emerge primarily in very large models, suggesting that chain-of-thought reasoning is an emergent capability of scale.

=== Paragraph LR1c ===
Methodologically, the authors craft few-shot prompts containing hand-written chain-of-thought annotations and evaluate the approach on three model families, with headline results on PaLM 540B. Benchmarks span arithmetic reasoning (GSM8K, SVAMP, ASDiv, AQuA, MAWPS), commonsense reasoning (CommonsenseQA, StrategyQA), and symbolic reasoning (last letter concatenation, coin flip). On GSM8K, PaLM 540B with chain-of-thought prompting reaches 56.9% accuracy versus 17.9% with standard prompting, a gain of 39 points, and the approach achieves state-of-the-art commonsense reasoning results without task-specific fine-tuning.

=== HEADING 2 ===
Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models

=== Paragraph LR2a ===
This paper, authored by Shunyu Yao and Dian Yu, was published at NeurIPS and has accumulated 420 citations according to the scholarly search. It extends chain-of-thought prompting into a framework for deliberate, search-based problem solving.

=== Paragraph LR2b ===
The key contribution is Tree of Thoughts (ToT), a framework that generalizes chain-of-thought prompting from a single linear sequence into a tree of coherent intermediate reasoning units called thoughts. The language model itself generates candidate thoughts, self-evaluates the promise of partial solutions, and explores the tree via breadth-first or depth-first search, looking ahead and backtracking when a line of reasoning proves unpromising. In this way, problem solving becomes an explicit search problem navigated by the model, again without any parameter updates.

=== Paragraph LR2c ===
The methodology comprises four components: thought decomposition, which breaks a problem into intermediate steps; thought generation, which proposes candidate thoughts by sampling or by prompting the model to propose options; state evaluation, in which the model scores partial solutions through value prompting or voting; and search, implemented as breadth-first or depth-first search over the thought tree. Experiments with GPT-4 cover three tasks requiring deliberate planning: on the Game of 24, ToT achieves a 74% success rate versus 4% for chain-of-thought prompting; on Creative Writing, human evaluators preferred ToT outputs 41% of the time versus 21% for chain-of-thought; and Mini Crosswords is additionally evaluated as a deliberate-planning puzzle.

=== HEADING 2 ===
Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models

=== Paragraph LR3a ===
This paper, authored by Xuezhi Wang and Jason Wei, was published at ICLR and has accumulated 650 citations according to the scholarly search. It improves chain-of-thought prompting through a better decoding strategy rather than better prompts.

=== Paragraph LR3b ===
The key contribution is self-consistency, a decoding strategy that replaces the greedy decoding conventionally used with chain-of-thought prompting. Instead of committing to a single sampled chain, the method samples a diverse set of reasoning paths at a non-zero temperature and then selects the answer that is most consistent across them by majority vote, effectively marginalizing out the sampled reasoning paths. The approach is fully unsupervised and exploits the intuition that a complex reasoning problem typically admits multiple distinct routes to the same correct answer, so correct paths tend to converge while erroneous paths diverge.

=== Paragraph LR3c ===
Methodologically, the procedure is threefold: prompt the model with chain-of-thought exemplars exactly as usual, sample multiple diverse reasoning paths instead of decoding greedily, and aggregate answers by majority vote. The improvement scales with the number of sampled paths and holds consistently across model families, including GPT-3, Codex, PaLM, and UL2. On GSM8K with PaLM 540B, self-consistency raises accuracy from 56.9% under greedy decoding to 74.4%, a gain of 17.5 points, and on ARC-challenge it improves accuracy from 85.2% to 89.2%.

=== HEADING 2 ===
Process Supervision for Mathematical Reasoning

=== Paragraph LR4a ===
This paper, authored by Hunter Lightman and Vineet Kosaraju, was published at ICML and has accumulated 280 citations according to the scholarly search. It shifts the focus from prompting and decoding to the supervision signal used to guide reasoning.

=== Paragraph LR4b ===
The key contribution is a detailed comparison of process supervision versus outcome supervision for training reward models that improve mathematical reasoning. Human labelers annotate each step of model-generated solutions as correct, incorrect, or neutral, and process reward models (PRMs) are trained to score each individual reasoning step. These PRMs are then used at test time to rank and select among candidate solutions through best-of-N sampling. The paper shows that step-level process supervision outperforms outcome supervision, which rewards only the final answer, and additionally yields better-calibrated confidence and more interpretable, step-localized feedback.

=== Paragraph LR4c ===
Experiments are conducted on the MATH benchmark. With best-of-1860 sampling, the process reward model guided selection solves 78.2% of problems from a representative subset, compared with 72.4% for an outcome reward model (ORM) under the same budget and 52.9% for the base model without reranking. At a smaller budget of 100 samples, the PRM reaches 71.5% versus 67.8% for the ORM, indicating that process supervision is more sample-efficient and that the two reward-modeling paradigms differ not only in peak performance but in how effectively they use test-time samples.

=== HEADING 2 ===
Scaling LLM Reasoning with Reinforcement Learning

=== Paragraph LR5a ===
This paper, authored by Alex Chen and Sarah Miller, was published at AAAI and has accumulated 190 citations according to the scholarly search. It investigates how reinforcement learning can scale reasoning capability by training the model itself, not just its prompts or decoding.

=== Paragraph LR5b ===
The key contribution is a comprehensive study of scaling reasoning through reinforcement learning, centered on a novel curriculum learning strategy combined with proximal policy optimization (PPO). A reward model trained on human preferences over reasoning traces provides step-level feedback, analogous to the process supervision of the previous paper, and the curriculum gradually advances training from simple single-step problems to complex multi-step reasoning tasks. The paper also reports scaling laws linking model size, reinforcement learning training compute, and reasoning performance.

=== Paragraph LR5c ===
The methodology combines several components: PPO with a KL penalty to keep updates stable and preserve output diversity, rejection sampling to generate high-quality training trajectories, the staged curriculum described above, and step-level rewards from the preference-trained reward model. On MATH, the reinforcement-learning-trained model reaches 67.3% accuracy versus 52.9% for a supervised fine-tuning baseline, and on ARC-challenge it attains 92.1%, reported as surpassing prior state of the art. The analysis finds an approximately log-linear relationship between training compute and reasoning performance, and that larger models benefit more from the reinforcement learning training.

=== HEADING 1 ===
Methodology Comparison

=== Paragraph MC1 ===
The five reviewed papers can be positioned according to where they intervene in the reasoning pipeline. Chain-of-thought prompting, Tree of Thoughts, and self-consistency all keep the model weights frozen and restructure inference alone: chain-of-thought does so through exemplar prompt design, Tree of Thoughts through explicit search over intermediate thoughts, and self-consistency through stochastic decoding and aggregation. Process supervision also keeps the generator frozen, but learns an external verifier from human step-level judgments to filter candidate solutions. The reinforcement learning study alone modifies the model's weights, transferring capability into training. The field therefore progresses from eliciting reasoning, to exploring the space of reasoning paths, to aggregating diverse paths, to verifying paths with a learned critic, and finally to learning to reason better directly.

=== Paragraph MC2 ===
A second axis of contrast is training requirement and supervision signal. Chain-of-thought, Tree of Thoughts, and self-consistency need no gradient updates; their guidance comes from hand-written exemplars, the model's own self-evaluation, or the model's own sampled outputs, respectively. The process supervision paper introduces human supervision at the granularity of individual steps, while the reinforcement learning paper derives a training signal from a reward model trained on human preferences over reasoning traces with step-level feedback. It is striking that both papers that employ supervision converge on step-level rather than outcome-level signals: the process supervision study explicitly shows process rewards beating outcome rewards by 78.2% to 72.4% under best-of-1860 on MATH, and the reinforcement learning study likewise adopts step-level rewards to stabilize learning. Step-level credit assignment appears to be the common ingredient whenever external feedback is available.

=== Paragraph MC3 ===
A third axis is where compute is spent. Self-consistency, Tree of Thoughts, and process-supervised best-of-N selection all purchase accuracy with test-time compute—more sampled paths, larger search trees, and more candidates N, respectively—as evidenced by self-consistency scaling with the number of sampled paths, the 70-point gain of Tree of Thoughts on the Game of 24, and the process reward model's continued improvement as the sampling budget grows from 100 to 1860. The reinforcement learning approach instead spends compute at training time; once training completes, the gains are internalized in the weights and available for every subsequent inference at no additional cost, and its log-linear compute-performance relationship suggests this may amortize best in the long run. Chain-of-thought prompting is the cheapest of all, adding only a longer prompt, but its gains emerge only in very large models and depend on the availability of good exemplars.

=== Paragraph MC4 ===
Despite these differences, the methodologies share a common core: every approach improves reasoning by producing explicit intermediate steps and, where possible, evaluating them. The benchmark overlap reinforces the connections: GSM8K anchors the prompting and decoding papers, where greedy chain-of-thought reaches 56.9% with PaLM 540B and self-consistency lifts that to 74.4%, while MATH anchors the supervision and reinforcement learning papers, whose base-model figure of 52.9% is identical, and ARC-challenge appears in both the self-consistency (89.2%) and reinforcement learning (92.1%) studies. This overlap implies that the gains from different approaches are largely complementary, and that stronger systems could combine reinforcement-learning-trained policies with inference-time decomposition, search, and verification.

=== Paragraph MC5 ===
Each mechanism also carries distinctive costs that explain why the approaches have coexisted rather than replaced one another. Chain-of-thought depends on manually written exemplars and delivers limited benefit to smaller models. Tree of Thoughts requires task-specific thought decomposition and evaluation prompting, and pays repeated inference costs for search. Self-consistency multiplies inference cost by the number of sampled paths. Process supervision depends on expensive human step-by-step annotation. Reinforcement learning demands careful engineering—KL penalties, rejection sampling, and a curriculum—to stabilize training and prevent catastrophic forgetting. Understanding these trade-offs is essential for choosing or combining approaches for a given deployment.

=== HEADING 1 ===
Conclusion

=== Paragraph C1 ===
The five papers reviewed here tell a coherent story: reasoning in large language models is not a single fixed capability but a family of capabilities that can be elicited by prompt design, amplified by decoding and search, verified by learned step-level evaluators, and ultimately improved by reinforcement learning training. Across the studies, the quantitative evidence is consistent—prompting raises GSM8K accuracy from 17.9% to 56.9% with PaLM 540B, search-based deliberation lifts Game of 24 success from 4% to 74%.

=== Paragraph C2 ===
Several common themes emerge. First, decomposition into explicit intermediate steps is the unifying mechanism across prompting, search, decoding, supervision, and reinforcement learning. Second, when supervision is used, step-level signals outperform outcome-level ones. Third, reasoning performance scales predictably with model size, with test-time compute, and with training compute, following approximately log-linear relationships in the reinforcement learning setting. Fourth, improvements generalize across domains—arithmetic, commonsense, symbolic, mathematical, and scientific reasoning—suggesting that the underlying capability is broadly transferable rather than benchmark-specific.

=== Paragraph C3 ===
Future research directions include reducing the cost of step-level supervision through automatically generated process rewards, unifying inference-time search with reinforcement-learning-trained policies, improving the efficiency of reasoning so that high quality does not require unbounded test-time compute, extending systematic evaluation beyond mathematics to science, code, and embodied planning, and developing theoretical understanding of why step-level credit assignment helps. As the field moves from eliciting reasoning to learning it, the synthesis of these threads—decomposition, search, verification, and reinforcement learning—points toward language models that reason deliberately, reliably, and at scale.

FINAL REMINDER: keep paragraphs in exactly this order; do not reorder or omit any; the title must be the very first block of the document. After building, verify both files exist at the exact target paths and report the verification results.
